01.note: Rabbi Hiyya of Parva visited the home of the Exilarch, and the household asked him whether an egg roasted by a gentile may be eaten. He answered that Hizkiyya and bar Kappara permit it while Rabbi Yohanan forbids it, and one Sage's view does not stand against two. Rav Zevid told them not to listen to him, because Abaye had said the law follows Rabbi Yohanan. They gave Rav Zevid a cup of spiced vinegar to drink, and he died.
01.why: The Gemara has just recorded the dispute over salted fish and roasted eggs prepared by gentiles; this visit shows the dispute being decided in practice, and the teaching that follows states plainly that a gentile's roasted egg is forbidden.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya of Parva
people.about: A visiting Sage asked about the roasted egg; he ruled that it is permitted, following the majority.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: Told the household not to listen, citing Abaye's ruling for Rabbi Yohanan; he died after drinking the vinegar they gave him.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage whose ruling Rav Zevid quotes: the law follows Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who forbids a gentile's roasted egg.

people.name: Hizkiyya
people.about: Sage who, with bar Kappara, permits a gentile's roasted egg.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who kept a large household.
Jewish law; the binding ruling on a question.

02.note: Two Sages were brought fish that looked like forbidden kinds. In Ginzak, Rabbi Akiva was shown a fish resembling a non-kosher sea creature; he shut it in a basket, saw that it shed scales as it struggled, and permitted it. In Tamduria, Rav Ashi was shown a fish that looked like an eel; he held it up to the daylight, saw thin scales on it, and permitted it.
02.why: The Gemara has been listing which fish are permitted and which forbidden; these visits show Sages settling doubtful cases by looking for scales, and the run of similar incidents continues afterward.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Sage who, in Ginzak, examined a doubtful fish in a basket and permitted it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who, in Tamduria, held a fish to the light and permitted it.

terms.meaning: Declared the fish kosher, fit for Jews to eat. A fish needs scales to be kosher, so finding scales settled the doubt.

03.note: In one place Rav Ashi was brought a fish that looked like a shefarnuna. He put it in a white vessel, saw the scales it shed against the white, and permitted it. In another place, Akra DeAgma, Rabba bar bar Hana was served tzahanta, a dish of small fish, and heard a man call it batei, the name of a non-kosher sea creature. The text here stops before saying what he did.
03.why: The Gemara is collecting incidents in which Sages tested doubtful fish; these two follow Rabbi Akiva's and Rav Ashi's earlier checks for scales.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who checked a doubtful fish in a white vessel and permitted it.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Sage served a fish dish while visiting Akra DeAgma, who heard it called by a non-kosher name.

terms.meaning: A dish made from small fish, often pickled or salted.
A kind of fish, named here because the doubtful fish resembled it.

03.flag: Combines the end of Rav Ashi's fish incident with only the opening of Rabba bar bar Hana's story, which is cut off; its ending is in the next segment.

04.note: Rabba bar bar Hana had been served a dish of small fish and heard a man call it by the name of a non-kosher sea creature. He reasoned that the name meant something non-kosher was in it, and he did not eat it that night. In the morning he examined the dish and found something non-kosher in it. He applied to himself the verse "No sin shall befall the righteous."
04.why: The Gemara is collecting incidents of Sages judging doubtful fish; this one ends with a Sage saved from eating forbidden food by a chance remark.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Sage who refused a fish dish after hearing it given a non-kosher name, and was proven right.

04.flag: Starts mid-story: the setting (being served tzahanta and hearing it called batei) is in the preceding segment.

05.note: Rav Huna bar Minyumi bought sky-blue dye from the household (the wife) of Rav Amram the pious and asked Rav Yosef whether he could rely on her; Rav Yosef did not know. Hanan the tailor met Rav Huna and said: how could poor Yosef know? It happened to me: I bought dye from the wife of Rabena'a, brother of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, and Rav Mattana did not know either. Then Rav Yehuda of Hagronya told me, "You have fallen into my hand," and quoted Shmuel: the wife of a haver is like a haver herself.
05.why: Rabbi Yohanan has just ruled that the slave of a haver is trusted like a haver; this story extends the same trust to his wife, and the Gemara then notes a teaching of the Sages that says both.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Minyumi
people.about: Bought sky-blue dye from Rav Amram's wife and sought a ruling on it.

people.name: Rav Amram the pious
people.about: Sage from whose household the dye was bought.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who did not know the answer to Rav Huna's question.

people.name: Hanan the tailor
people.about: Told Rav Huna of his own similar case and how it was answered.

people.name: Rav Yehuda of Hagronya
people.about: Answered Hanan, quoting Shmuel that a haver's wife is trusted like a haver.

terms.meaning: The blue dye required for one thread of ritual fringes. It was easy to counterfeit, so it could be bought only from a trusted seller.
A member of a fellowship committed to careful observance, especially of purity and tithing laws, and so trusted on such matters.

06.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar told of a woman who was married to a haver and used to tie his phylacteries on his hand. Later she married a tax collector, and she used to tie his tax-seals on his hand.
06.why: Rabbi Meir has said that a haver's wife who remarries an ordinary man need not take on the haver's commitments anew, and Rabbi Yehuda disagrees; this case backs Rabbi Yehuda, showing a wife follows the ways of whoever she is married to.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Sage who tells the incident of the woman.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage who rules that such people must take on the haver's commitments from the start.

terms.meaning: A member of a fellowship committed to careful observance, especially of purity and tithing laws.
Tefillin: small leather boxes containing Torah verses, bound on the arm and head during weekday prayer.
Seals or tags a tax collector used in his work, here tied on his hand the way phylacteries are.

07.note: A ship carrying tzahanta, a small-fish dish, came to Sikhra. Rav Huna bar Hinnana went out, saw scales among the fish, and permitted it. Rava objected: who permits in such a case, in a place where scales are common? Shofar blasts went out from Rava's court forbidding the fish, and shofar blasts went out from Rav Huna bar Hinnana's court permitting it.
07.why: The Gemara is asking when fish brine and pieces of fish may be trusted, and Rav Pappa requires every fish to be recognizable; after this case the Gemara gives two versions of whether Rav Huna bar Hinnana permitted only the brine or the fish themselves.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hinnana
people.about: Sage who saw scales on the ship's fish and permitted them.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who objected and forbade the fish.

terms.meaning: A dish made from small fish.
Blowing the shofar (ram's horn) was how a court publicly announced its ruling.

08.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had stomach pain and asked whether anyone knew if gentiles' apple wine is permitted. Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei said that his father once had stomach pain, was brought gentiles' apple wine seventy years old, drank it and was cured. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: you had all this in your hand and let me suffer! They searched and found a gentile with three hundred jugs of seventy-year-old apple wine. He drank and was cured, and said: Blessed is the Omnipresent who delivered His world to keepers.
08.why: A teaching of the Sages has just said that gentiles' apple wine from a storehouse is permitted, while apple wine sold in the market is forbidden because grape wine may be mixed in; this story shows the leniency relied on.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Sage, called simply Rabbi, who needed apple wine for his stomach pain.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that his father had drunk gentiles' apple wine as a cure.

terms.meaning: A name for God.
A drink made from apples. Unlike grape wine, it is not used in idol worship, so the question was only whether grape wine had been mixed in.

09.note: Rabbi Yehuda told of a case in the town of Rimon: the maidservant of a violent man threw a stillborn baby into a pit. A priest came and looked into the pit to see whether it was male or female. The case came before the Sages, and they ruled the priest ritually pure, because martens and polecats are common there.
09.why: The Gemara has argued that an uncertainty cannot override a certainty; this case is raised as an objection, since the Sages let the doubt that animals dragged the body away outweigh the certainty that it was thrown in.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage who reports the case.

people.name: a priest
people.about: Looked into the pit; a priest must avoid the impurity of a corpse.

terms.meaning: Not made impure. A priest who is under the same roof or over a corpse becomes impure and is barred from Temple service and holy food.
Small animals that might have dragged the body out of the pit before the priest arrived.

10.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recalled walking on the road behind Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who found a ring bearing the figure of a dragon. He met a gentile boy and said nothing to him. Then he met an adult gentile and told him to revoke the ring's idolatrous status, but the man would not. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar slapped him, and he revoked it.
10.why: The Sages have just defined the dragon figure that marks an object as idolatrous; from this incident the Gemara learns that a gentile can revoke another's idol, that only one who understands idol worship can do so, and that it works even against his will.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Passes on the account in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Was walking with Rabbi Elazar HaKappar and tells what happened.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
people.about: Found the ring and made an adult gentile revoke its status.

terms.meaning: To cancel an object's status as an idol, done by a gentile through an act of disrespect toward it; after that a Jew may use it.
An image the Sages treat as a sign that an object was made for idol worship.

11.note: A teaching of the Sages forbids building a house, porch, courtyard, table or seven-branched lampstand copying those of the Temple, though a lamp of five, six or eight branches is allowed. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds that one may not make one of wood either, as the Hasmoneans did. The Sages answered him: the Hasmonean lampstand was made of iron spits covered with tin; when they grew richer they made it of silver, and when richer still, of gold.
11.why: Abaye has explained that the Torah forbids copying only things whose likeness can truly be reproduced; this teaching supports him, since the Temple's furnishings can be copied exactly, unlike the moon figures Rabban Gamliel drew.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
people.about: Sage who forbids even a wooden lampstand, citing the Hasmoneans.

terms.meaning: The main building of the Temple in Jerusalem.
The priestly family who led the revolt against the Greeks and rededicated the Temple, the events remembered at Hanukkah.
The Temple's seven-branched lampstand, the Menorah.

11.flag: Mostly a legal teaching; the only narrative is a brief historical report of how the Hasmonean candelabrum was made.

12.note: The house of King Yannai was destroyed, and gentiles set up stones to the god Mercury in it. Later, other gentiles who did not worship Mercury took the stones and paved paths and streets with them. Some Rabbis kept off those paths and others did not. Rabbi Yohanan said: the son of holy ones walks on them, and should we keep away? The Gemara explains that this was Rabbi Menahem son of Rabbi Simai, called so because he would not even look at the image on a coin.
12.why: The Gemara has been defining which stones count as part of a Mercury pile; after the story it gives the reasoning on each side, whether an idolatrous offering can ever lose its forbidden status, or whether stones are not offerings at all.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: King whose ruined house the gentiles used.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who argued against avoiding the paved paths.

people.name: Rabbi Menahem son of Rabbi Simai
people.about: Called the son of holy ones; he walked on the paths, though he would not even look at the image on a coin.

terms.meaning: A Roman god worshipped by adding stones to a heap or by throwing stones at it; the stones count as forbidden idol offerings.

13.note: A philosopher asked Rabban Gamliel: your Torah calls God a jealous God, so why is He jealous of idol worshippers but not of the idol itself? Rabban Gamliel told a parable of a king whose son named his dog after his father and swore by it: the king is angry with the son, not the dog. The philosopher said the idol has real power: when his city burned, only its temple survived. Rabban Gamliel answered with a king who wages war on the living, not the dead. Then let God destroy it, said the philosopher. Rabban Gamliel replied that people worship the sun, moon, stars and rivers: should God destroy His world because of fools? He cited a verse from Zephaniah: people worship humans too, so must humanity be cut off?
13.why: The Gemara has just taught that the world follows its course and sinners will be judged later, even when God seems to allow wrongdoing; this exchange carries the theme to idols, which God lets stand.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Sage who answers the philosopher's questions with parables and a verse.

people.name: a philosopher
people.about: A non-Jewish thinker who challenges Rabban Gamliel about God's jealousy and idols.

terms.meaning: A short illustrative tale, here about a king, used to explain how God acts.
A phrase from Deuteronomy describing God's response to idol worship.

14.note: In Neharde'a a Jew and a gentile trod grapes together to make wine, and Shmuel put off ruling on that wine for three Festivals, when the Sages gathered. The Gemara asks why. It rejects the idea that he hoped to find a teacher who sided with Rabbi Natan, which would forbid even profiting from the wine, since Rabbi Natan forbids only a gentile's touch by hand. Rather, says the Gemara, he hoped to find one who sided with Rabbi Shimon, so he could permit the wine even for drinking. The text does not say how he finally ruled.
14.why: A gifted child has just ruled that a Jew may tread grapes alongside a gentile, since a foot's touch does not make wine a libation; Shmuel's long hesitation over a real case shows the question was far from simple.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who delayed his ruling on the wine for three Festivals.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: Sage who forbids wine a gentile measured by hand but permits it by foot.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Sage who permits wine a gentile touched without meaning to offer it.

terms.meaning: The pilgrimage holidays, when Sages gathered and questions could be discussed.
A Sage of the earlier period whose teachings carry authority; Shmuel sought one supporting a ruling.
Wine poured out in idol worship. Wine a gentile may have offered this way is forbidden to Jews.

15.note: In Biram a gentile climbing down a palm tree with a palm branch touched some wine with the tip of the branch, without meaning to. Rav permitted the owners to sell the wine to gentiles. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi asked him: didn't you, Master, say that even a one-day-old gentile baby makes wine a libation by touching it? Rav answered: I said it forbids drinking the wine; did I say it forbids benefit from it?
15.why: The Gemara has been asking what a gentile's unintended touch does to wine, in Shmuel's case; Rav's ruling separates drinking from profiting, and the Gemara then turns to examine his statement about the baby.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who let the wine be sold to gentiles.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: With Rav Asi, challenged Rav using his own statement.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: With Rav Kahana, challenged Rav using his own statement.

terms.meaning: Wine poured out in idol worship. Wine a gentile may have offered this way is forbidden to Jews.
Making any use or profit of something, such as selling it, as opposed to eating or drinking it.

16.note: In Mehoza a gentile walked into a Jew's shop and asked for wine. Told there was none, he put his hand in a bucket of wine, stirred it, and said: isn't this wine? In anger the shopkeeper threw it into a barrel. Rava permitted selling the barrel to gentiles; Rav Huna bar Hinnana and Rav Huna son of Rav Nahman forbade it, and each court announced its ruling with shofar blasts. When Rav Huna son of Rav Nahman came to Mehoza, Rava had his attendant shut the gates so they would not be disturbed. Asked about such a case, Rava said even benefit is forbidden; challenged, he said he had permitted the barrel except for the value of the stirred wine.
16.why: The Gemara is asking whether a gentile's touch without intent to worship forbids wine; afterward Rava recalls that Abaye pressed him with Shmuel's and Rabbi Yohanan's rulings forbidding stirred wine, and with a teaching of the Sages.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage in Mehoza who permitted the barrel to be sold to gentiles.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hinnana
people.about: Sage who disagreed with Rava and forbade the sale.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage who forbade the sale and came to Mehoza to question Rava.

people.name: Rav Elyakim
people.about: Rava's attendant, told to shut the gates.

terms.meaning: Blowing the shofar (ram's horn) was how a court publicly announced its ruling.
Wine poured out in idol worship. Wine a gentile may have offered this way is forbidden to Jews.
Making any use or profit of something, such as selling it, as opposed to drinking it.

17.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza and Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai were sitting drinking wine when a man came by, and they asked him to pour for them. After he poured, it turned out he was a gentile. One Sage forbade the wine even for benefit; the other permitted it even for drinking. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said both ruled well: the gentile might have thought such Sages surely drink wine, and offered it; or he might have thought Sages would never ask a gentile to pour wine, so it must be liquor, and not offered it. The Gemara adds that it was night, the wine was new and hard to smell, and he poured without touching it.
17.why: The Gemara has just concluded that wine a gentile stirred is forbidden even for benefit; this case asks what happens when he pours without touching, and ends with the rule that the Sages did not forbid wine moved by a gentile's force without intent.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza
people.about: One of the two Sages drinking wine who asked the stranger to pour.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai
people.about: The other Sage at the table.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Sage who said both rulings were sound and explained each.

terms.meaning: Here shikhra, a beer-like drink not made from grapes, which idol worshippers did not pour as offerings.
Wine poured out in idol worship. Wine a gentile may have offered this way is forbidden to Jews.

18.note: Reish Lakish came to Bozrah and saw Jews eating untithed produce, and he forbade it to them. He also saw Jews drinking water that gentiles bowed down to, and he forbade it too. He came before Rabbi Yohanan, who told him: while your coat is still on you, go back and retract. Bozrah is not the Bezer named in the Torah, so its produce needs no tithing, and public water is not made forbidden. The text does not say whether he went back.
18.why: The Gemara has just told of Rabbi Yirmeya forbidding diluted wine on a visit to Savta; afterward it notes that Rabbi Yohanan's rule here, that public water cannot be made forbidden, matches what he taught elsewhere.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage who forbade produce and water to the Jews of Bozrah.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who told Reish Lakish to go back and retract both rulings.

terms.meaning: Crops grown in the Land of Israel from which the required portions for priests, Levites and the poor have not been set aside; eating them is forbidden.
A city named in the Torah as a city of refuge, in the land of Israel; Rabbi Yohanan says Bozrah is a different place.

19.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba came to Gavla. He saw Jewish women pregnant by gentiles who had been circumcised but had not yet immersed for conversion, Jews drinking wine that gentiles had diluted, and Jews eating lupines that gentiles had cooked, and he said nothing to them. He came before Rabbi Yohanan, who told him: go and declare their children mamzerim, their wine forbidden as libation wine, and their lupines forbidden as food cooked by gentiles, because they are not people learned in Torah.
19.why: The Gemara then explains each instruction by Rabbi Yohanan's own rulings: a convert needs both circumcision and immersion, a child of a gentile and a Jewish woman is a mamzer, and people unlearned in Torah need stricter fences.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Sage who saw the practices in Gavla and said nothing.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who told him to declare all three forbidden.

terms.meaning: Dipping in a ritual bath, the final step of conversion; until then the man is still legally a gentile.
Children of a forbidden union, who may not marry ordinary Jews.
Wine that may have been poured out in idol worship, forbidden to Jews; here extended to wine a gentile diluted.
A rabbinic ban on certain foods cooked by non-Jews.

20.note: An etrog fell into a barrel of wine, and a gentile jumped up to take it out. Rav Ashi told the people there: hold his hand so that he does not stir the wine, and tip the barrel until the wine has drained out.
20.why: Rav Kahana has just ruled that a gentile should not be allowed to bring grapes to the winepress in the first place, as a fence; Rav Ashi's instruction is another way of keeping a gentile's touch from making a Jew's wine forbidden.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who told the bystanders how to save the wine.

terms.meaning: A citron, the fruit used in the Sukkot festival.
A gentile's stirring of wine is treated like touching it in worship, which can make it forbidden to Jews.
